Title: [from] Surprising Saturn
Author: by Liz Huyck
Content: Welcome to `text(Saturn)`
`text(Saturn)` is the `text(sixth)` planet from the sun, and the `text(second)` largest planet in our solar system. It's `95` times more massive than `text(Earth)`, and `9` times as wide.

A year on `text(Saturn)` (the time it takes to go around the sun `text(once)`) is `text(29.5 Earth years)` long. But the `text(days)` are short. `text(Saturn)` is spinning very quickly, so it has a new day every `text(10.5 hours)`.

`text(Saturn)` is very far away. It orbits about `text(880 million miles)` ... from the sun. Even a very fast spaceship would take ... `text(years)` to get there... Phone signals, traveling at the speed of light, take over an `text(hour)` to make the trip. So phone calls to `text(Saturn)` would have long pauses.

The planet gets its name from `text(Saturn)`, the Roman god of agriculture and father of `text(Jupiter)`. `text(Saturday)` is also named for him, so `text(Saturday)` is a great `text(day)` to look at `text(Saturn)`.
It Has No Surface
Like `text(Jupiter)`, ... `text(Saturn)` is a gas planet. That means it has no solid surface - it's a big ball of cloud. So after you've come all this way, you won't be able to land on it!

You also probably shouldn't try to fly through it. Even though it's made of gas, `text(Saturn)` is huge and has strong gravity. If a spaceship tried to fly through, gas molecules would rub against the ship and heat it up - a lot. Then the force of all the gas pressing in would crush it like a tin can.

What kind of gas is it? `text(Saturn)` is mostly hydrogen, helium, and water vapor, with clouds of ammonia and other chemicals. Near `text(Saturn's)` center, the pressure is so intense that hydrogen is squashed into a metallic liquid. At the very center, it may have a small core of rock, like the pit in a cherry. But we don't know for sure.
It Would Float in a Bathtub
`text(Saturn)` is enormous, but it's not very dense. It's kind of like a foamy marshmallow, or a big cloud of haze. So if you could find a bathtub big enough, `text(Saturn)` would float! ...
It Wears Rings

`text(Saturn's)` most noticeable feature is its spectacular rings. The rings are not solid. They are made up of small bits of ice and dust... But they are very thin - only about `text(30 feet)` (`text(10 )`m) thick. They're so thin that up close, you can see through them.
`text(Saturn)` did not always have rings. They probably formed when a couple of small moons or comets smashed together, scattering ice and dust in a ring around the planet.

`text(Saturn)` is famous for its rings, but it's not the only ringed planet. `text(Jupiter)`, `text(Uranus)`, and `text(Neptune)` also have rings, though they are small and faint. Some scientists think that `text(Earth)` also may have `text(once)` had a rocky ring...
Many Moons

`text(Saturn)` is rich in rings, and also in moons - it has at least `146`. There are `text(eight)` big `text(ones)` and `text(dozens)` of smaller ones. Some orbit close to the planet. Some are `text(millions of miles)` away. And some tumble around in the rings.

`text(Saturn's)` moons are mostly ice and rock dust. Most are quite small, less than `text(100 miles)` (`text(160 km)`) across. The small moons inside `text(Saturn's)` rings are called shepherd moons. They make gaps in the rings by sweeping up ice. They also make waves. The rings are also full of tiny “moonlets,” the beginnings of new moons.
A few groups of small moons orbit quite far from `text(Saturn)`. These distant moons are probably pieces of captured asteroids - giant balls of ice and rock that wandered too close to the planet.
`text(Two)` moons, Titan and Enceladus, have underground oceans beneath icy outer shells. Titan has methane lakes and even an atmosphere.
